title: Optimal Dynamic Cooling of Multiple Qubits
authors: Mattia Reda, Massimiliano Sacchi, Chiara Macchiavello, Giacomo Guarnieri
abstract: We solve the closed-system problem of cooling $M$ qubits, selected from $N$ identical thermal qubits, to the lowest common local temperature allowed by unitarity. The optimal protocol consists of two conceptually distinct steps. First, a passive rearrangement assigns the largest eigenvalues of the initial state to target sectors of lowest Hamming weight, thereby minimizing the total target energy. Second, a target-only complex-Hadamard transformation within each fixed-Hamming-weight subspace equalizes the one-qubit target marginals without changing any target-sector probability or the total energy. Consequently, imposing a common local temperature costs neither cooling depth nor additional work: the constrained optimum coincides with the unconstrained passive minimum for every $N>M$ and every initial temperature. The complex-Hadamard correction may nevertheless be costly at the circuit level. We therefore derive an exact arithmetic criterion for when the same optimum can be attained by a temperature-independent computational-basis permutation alone, and exhaustively classify the resulting finite-size islands of feasibility for $M+2\leq N\leq 128$. At isolated temperatures, further optimal permutations can arise through numerical cancellations between different thermal eigenvalue shells. These alternative realizations may reduce implementation complexity, but they cannot improve the cooling curve already attained by the universal protocol. We also derive the exact cooling curve, prove that at least two ancillary qubits are necessary and sufficient for nontrivial cooling, and show that joint many-target cooling can strictly outperform parallel single-target strategies.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory for optimally cooling multiple qubits by treating the system as a single closed unit. It proves that a global unitary transformation achieves the lowest possible target temperature, outperforming parallel cooling strategies. The methodology involves spectral analysis and combinatorial constraints to determine when simpler, permutation-based protocols can match this theoretical optimum.
main_problem: The paper addresses the closed-system problem of optimally cooling $M$ target qubits selected from a larger pool of $N$ identical thermal qubits to achieve the lowest common local temperature allowed by unitarity.
main_result: A universal optimal protocol exists that achieves the minimum possible mean target energy, and this global strategy strictly outperforms parallel single-target cooling methods. The analysis also provides exact criteria for when simpler permutation-only protocols suffice.
method: The authors combine spectral analysis of the initial state with optimization techniques to derive an optimal unitary transformation ($U_*$) composed of a passive rearrangement and a complex-Hadamard correction. They use graph theory concepts (hypergraph coloring) to analyze feasibility conditions for permutations.
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ identical, noninteracting qubits initially prepared in a Gibbs state $ho( eta)$. The cooling process is modeled as the evolution under a global unitary transformation acting on this register.
key_observables: Local target temperature, mean target energy ($p_\star(P_1)$), and the cooling curve depth ($\xi_M^\star$).
important_parameters: $N$ (total qubits), $M$ (target qubits), initial inverse temperature $ eta$, and the ratio of global vs. parallel cooling performance.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system remains closed, and while a complex-Hadamard correction is optimal, alternative permutation realizations are analyzed for implementation simplicity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate dynamic cooling protocols using global unitaries on $N$ qubits to cool $M$ targets; they also show resource allocation diagrams comparing global vs. parallel target populations for specific $(N, M)$ pairs.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the optimal protocol via two steps (passive rearrangement and Hadamard correction). It then derives necessary and sufficient arithmetic criteria for achieving this optimum using only permutations, classifying feasibility islands. Finally, it provides quantitative bounds on the achievable cooling depth by comparing global vs. parallel strategies.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical tools to analyze resource optimization in quantum thermodynamics, specifically quantifying how collective coupling (global unitary) improves energy extraction compared to independent local operations, which is highly relevant for designing efficient quantum refrigerators or thermalization protocols.
